topics.label: Lecture introduction and framing
topics.groupedBecause: The opening frames the lecture as an integration of previously introduced immune cells and molecules.

topics.label: Principles of innate danger recognition
topics.groupedBecause: These subtopics explain how innate cells distinguish danger through molecular patterns and appropriately localised, germline-encoded receptors.

topics.label: Toll-like receptor recognition and signalling
topics.groupedBecause: These subtopics explain how Toll-like receptors translate microbial recognition into immune responses suited to the location of infection.

topics.label: Non-TLR pathways linking danger recognition to inflammation
topics.groupedBecause: These subtopics show how alternative danger-sensing pathways activate inflammation and can contribute to inflammatory disease.

topics.label: Sentinel-driven inflammation and leukocyte recruitment
topics.groupedBecause: These subtopics trace how activated sentinel cells generate inflammatory signals that mobilise leukocytes to the site of infection.

topics.label: Lymphatic transport and adaptive immune priming
topics.groupedBecause: This subtopic explains how lymphatic drainage carries evidence of tissue infection to lymph nodes for adaptive immune activation.

topics.label: Excessive systemic inflammation and septic shock
topics.groupedBecause: This subtopic examines how excessive inflammatory activation becomes a life-threatening systemic response.

topics.label: Mechanisms of inflammation resolution
topics.groupedBecause: This subtopic explains how declining inflammatory stimulation and active inhibitory signals bring an immune response to an end.

topics.label: Tissue repair and persistent inflammation
topics.groupedBecause: These subtopics examine why inflamed tissue may recover or remain chronically inflamed, with granulomas illustrating containment when infection cannot be cleared.

topics.label: Lecture close and next lecture
topics.groupedBecause: The closing ends the lecture and announces complement as the next lecture's subject.
